observations.title: Mixed use of marinara.apiFetch and raw fetch for lorebook operations
observations.technical_explanation: The sweep loop uses marinara.apiFetch for the PATCH unlock call but switches to a raw browser fetch for the DELETE call on the same lorebook endpoint. Both target the same-origin local Marinara API. The raw fetch omits any explicit headers or credentials handling that marinara.apiFetch may provide, which could cause the DELETE to behave differently from other calls if Marinara requires authentication headers. This is a consistency concern, not a security exfiltration issue.
observations.layman_explanation: The code uses two slightly different methods to talk to the local app when deleting and unlocking lorebook entries. It works but is inconsistent and could fail silently if the app needs special headers.
observations.developer_action: Use marinara.apiFetch consistently for all lorebook API calls, including the DELETE, to ensure authentication and header handling match the rest of the extension.

observations.title: Multiple dependency advisories concentrated in undici and fastify
observations.technical_explanation: Eight OSV-Scanner advisories were raised against this lockfile. The runtime dependencies include undici and fastify, both of which have accumulated numerous advisories. The project server binds to 127.0.0.1 only and makes outbound HTTP requests to user-configured endpoints (local Ollama or an optional external OpenAI-compatible API). This deployment model substantially limits the practical exploitability of most known dependency vulnerabilities in these libraries. A single dependency update pass would likely resolve all or most of the flagged advisories.
observations.layman_explanation: The project uses several libraries that have known security updates available. Because the server only runs locally and only connects to services you set up yourself, the practical danger is low. The developer should update these libraries to their latest patched versions.
observations.developer_action: Run npm audit or npm update to identify and upgrade all affected dependencies to patched versions, then regenerate the lockfile and verify the application still works.

observations.title: Static git command for build version identification
observations.technical_explanation: The execSync invocation passes a literal command string with no external data. The cwd is constrained to a discovered repository root, and failure falls through to a content-hash fallback. This matches the stated purpose of producing a build version string for diagnostics.
observations.layman_explanation: The extension runs a simple, unchangeable git command to label the current build. It is used only for showing version information and is not influenced by any user input.

observations.title: User-initiated auto-start toggle with clear disclosure
observations.technical_explanation: All four candidates belong to a single user-facing auto-start toggle triggered by pressing 'A' in the console menu. The toggle writes or removes a batch launcher in the Windows startup directory that re-runs start.ps1 minimized. The launcher content is plainly visible in the script, the action is gated behind explicit user input, and the console provides immediate confirmation and instructions to disable. No covert installation, no obfuscation, and the persistence is limited to re-launching the project's own local server.
observations.layman_explanation: The four flagged lines are all part of one feature: an optional auto-start switch the user turns on or off by pressing A. When on, it creates a startup shortcut for the local memory server; when off, it removes it. The script clearly tells the user what it did and how to undo it.

limitations: This advisory review cannot prove the absence of unknown behavior.
